claim: A multispecies coalescent model for quantitative traits allows for evolutionary inferences at micro- and macroevolutionary scales.
source: We present a multispecies coalescent model for quantitative traits that allows for evolutionary inferences at micro- and macroevolutionary scales.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The multispecies coalescent model for quantitative traits can incorporate genealogical discordance underlying a quantitative trait.
source: A major advantage of this model is its ability to incorporate genealogical discordance underlying a quantitative trait.
evidence: This is stated as a major advantage of the model in the abstract.

claim: Discordance causes a decrease in the expected trait covariance between more closely related species relative to more distantly related species.
source: We show that discordance causes a decrease in the expected trait covariance between more closely related species relative to more distantly related species.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by theoretical derivations and simulations shown in the manuscript.

claim: Unaccounted discordance can lead to an overestimation of a trait's evolutionary rate.
source: If unaccounted for, this outcome can lead to an overestimation of a trait's evolutionary rate, to a decrease in its phylogenetic signal, and to errors when examining shifts in mean trait values.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through simulations in Figure 6a.

claim: Unaccounted discordance can lead to a decrease in a trait's phylogenetic signal.
source: If unaccounted for, this outcome can lead to an overestimation of a trait's evolutionary rate, to a decrease in its phylogenetic signal, and to errors when examining shifts in mean trait values.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through simulations in Figure 6b showing decreasing Pagel's λ with increasing ILS.

claim: Unaccounted discordance can lead to errors when examining shifts in mean trait values.
source: If unaccounted for, this outcome can lead to an overestimation of a trait's evolutionary rate, to a decrease in its phylogenetic signal, and to errors when examining shifts in mean trait values.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through phylogenetic ANOVA results in Figure 7.

claim: The number of loci controlling a quantitative trait is irrelevant to the trends caused by discordance.
source: The number of loci controlling a quantitative trait appears to be irrelevant to all trends reported, and discordance also affected discrete, threshold traits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through simulations with varying numbers of loci (5, 15, 25, 50, 100) showing similar trends.

claim: Discordance affects discrete, threshold traits.
source: The number of loci controlling a quantitative trait appears to be irrelevant to all trends reported, and discordance also affected discrete, threshold traits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through threshold trait simulations shown in Figure 8.

claim: Phylogenetic comparative methods model traits as evolving along a phylogeny.
source: Phylogenetic comparative methods model traits as evolving along a phylogeny, and therefore often require one, or sometimes multiple, species trees as input (Pagel, 1999; O'Meara, 2012; Hahn and Nakhleh, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Phylogenomic studies have revealed topological discordance between gene trees to be pervasive across the tree of life.
source: In contrast to the high levels of support provided by genome-scale data, phylogenomic studies have also revealed topological discordance between gene trees to be pervasive across the tree of life (Pollard et al., 2006; White et al., 2009; Hobolth et al., 2011; Brawand et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Suh et al., 2015; Pease et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations from phylogenomic studies.

claim: Gene trees can disagree with one another and with the species tree due to incomplete lineage sorting (ILS).
source: Gene trees can disagree with one another and with the species tree because of technical reasons — for example, model misspecification, low phylogenetic signal, or the mis-identification of paralogs as orthologs — but also as a result of biological phenomena such as incomplete lineage sorting (ILS), introgression, and horizontal gene transfer (Maddison, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: ILS occurs when lineages from the same population do not coalesce in that population, but instead coalesce in a more ancestral population.
source: Going backwards in time, ILS is said to occur when lineages from the same population do not coalesce in that population, but instead coalesce in a more ancestral population.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction.

claim: ILS is well-studied due to its conduciveness to mathematical characterization.
source: Among the latter, ILS is well-studied due to its conduciveness to mathematical characterization (Hudson, 1983; Tajima, 1983; Pamilo and Nei, 1988), in addition to being an inevitable result of population processes (Edwards, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ILS is an inevitable result of population processes.
source: Among the latter, ILS is well-studied due to its conduciveness to mathematical characterization (Hudson, 1983; Tajima, 1983; Pamilo and Nei, 1988), in addition to being an inevitable result of population processes (Edwards, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Hemiplasy is the production of a homoplasy-like pattern by a non-homoplastic event.
source: Hemiplasy is the production of a homoplasy-like pattern by a non-homoplastic event (Avise and Robinson, 2008), generally because a character-state transition has occurred on a discordant gene tree.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Hemiplasy generally occurs because a character-state transition has occurred on a discordant gene tree.
source: Hemiplasy is the production of a homoplasy-like pattern by a non-homoplastic event (Avise and Robinson, 2008), generally because a character-state transition has occurred on a discordant gene tree.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the definition of hemiplasy.

claim: At the molecular level, hemiplasy can cause apparent substitution rate variation.
source: At the molecular level, hemiplasy can cause apparent substitution rate variation, can spuriously increase the detection of positive selection in coding sequences, and can lead to artefactual signals of convergence (Mendes and Hahn, 2016; Mendes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Hemiplasy can spuriously increase the detection of positive selection in coding sequences.
source: At the molecular level, hemiplasy can cause apparent substitution rate variation, can spuriously increase the detection of positive selection in coding sequences, and can lead to artefactual signals of convergence (Mendes and Hahn, 2016; Mendes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Hemiplasy can lead to artefactual signals of convergence.
source: At the molecular level, hemiplasy can cause apparent substitution rate variation, can spuriously increase the detection of positive selection in coding sequences, and can lead to artefactual signals of convergence (Mendes and Hahn, 2016; Mendes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In datasets with high levels of gene tree discordance, the fraction of all substitutions that are hemiplastic can be quite high.
source: In datasets with high levels of gene tree discordance, the fraction of all substitutions that are hemiplastic can be quite high (Copetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Under Brownian motion, trait values from multiple species exhibit a multivariate normal distribution with the covariance structure given by the phylogeny.
source: Under BM, trait values from multiple species will exhibit a multivariate normal distribution with the covariance structure given by the phylogeny (Felsenstein, 1973).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Under Brownian motion, the variances within species and covariances between species are given by V = σ2T.
source: More specifically, in the case of n species, the variances within species and covariances between species are given by V = σ2T, the variance-covariance matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a description of the Brownian motion model.

claim: The selection coefficient on an individual allele is proportional to its effect size.
source: Although many quantitative traits may be under selection, the selection coefficient on an individual allele is proportional its effect size (Keightley and Hill, 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Loci with small effects will experience very small selection coefficients.
source: This implies that loci with small effects will experience very small selection coefficients, and that neutral expectations for genealogical quantities should still be justified.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the proportionality between selection coefficient and effect size.

claim: For any N > 0, the single-species variance under the coalescent model will be larger than that expected under BM.
source: It is easy to see that for any N > 0, the single-species variance under the coalescent model will be larger than that expected under BM.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated through mathematical comparison of Equations 1 and 2.

claim: Traditional phylogenetic models such as BM do not consider the variation that exists in ancestral populations prior to speciation.
source: This is a curious, yet not unexpected result: traditional phylogenetic models such as BM do not consider the variation that exists in ancestral populations prior to speciation (Gillespie and Langley, 1979; Edwards and Beerli, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Expected covariances between species under the coalescent and BM models are exactly equivalent in the absence of genealogical discordance.
source: Conversely, expected covariances between species under both models should be exactly equivalent in the absence of genealogical discordance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated through mathematical comparison.

claim: Expected trait values in the coalescent are not exactly the same as those expected under the classical BM model, even in the absence of genealogical discordance and given a fixed phylogeny.
source: However, expected trait values in the coalescent are not exactly the same as those expected under the classical BM model, even in the absence of genealogical discordance and given a fixed phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the results section.

claim: Expected variances differ between the coalescent and BM models even in the absence of genealogical discordance.
source: While expected covariances will be identical between models if no genealogical discordance is present, expected variances will still differ; this difference will be accentuated with larger ancestral population sizes.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the results section.

claim: The difference in expected variances between coalescent and BM models will be accentuated with larger ancestral population sizes.
source: While expected covariances will be identical between models if no genealogical discordance is present, expected variances will still differ; this difference will be accentuated with larger ancestral population sizes.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the results section.

claim: There was an overall good match between the observed and expected variances and covariances in the simulations.
source: We observed an overall good match between the observed and expected variances and covariances (Figure 4 and Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 4 and 5a showing close agreement between expected and observed values.

claim: Larger ancestral population sizes result in higher variances and covariances under the coalescent model.
source: Under the coalescent model, larger ancestral population sizes make coalescent waiting times longer, and result not only in more ILS and more gene tree discordance, but also in taller trees on average. As expected (Equations 2–4), data sets simulated with larger N therefore had higher variances and covariances (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 4a-b.

claim: The 'deep coalescence' (DC) effect occurs due to the increase in average gene tree height, relative to the species tree height, under the coalescent model with large population sizes.
source: The DC effect occurs due to the increase in average gene tree height, relative to the species tree height, under the coalescent model with large population sizes (cf. Gillespie and Langley, 1979).
evidence: This is stated as a definition and explanation in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The deep coalescence effect is not due to discordance.
source: We stress that (i) this effect is not due to discordance, and (ii) not only variances, but covariances among lineages that share a history in the species tree, are affected.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the results section.

claim: The number of loci did not influence variances and covariances.
source: The number of loci did not influence variances and covariances (results not shown), which is expected.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on simulation results.

claim: Under the coalescent model, gene tree discordance causes the covariance between non-sister species to increase with more ILS relative to the covariance between sister species.
source: Finally, under the coalescent model, gene tree discordance does have an effect: the covariance between species A and C (and between B and C) increases with more ILS relative to the covariance between species A and B (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 5a.

claim: Discordant gene trees offer the opportunity for non-sister species to have a shared history, and covariance increases.
source: Recall that when there is no discordance there is no covariance between non-sister species, because they do not share an evolutionary history. Discordant gene trees offer the opportunity for non-sister species to have a shared history, and covariance increases.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation in the results section.

claim: The effect of hemiplasy on continuous traits is to make covariances between different pairs of species converge on the same value.
source: Ultimately, the effect of hemiplasy on continuous traits is to make covariances between different pairs of species converge on the same value (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 5b.

claim: The concordant topology was always the most common in the simulations.
source: We emphasize that the aforementioned effects were observed despite the fact that the concordant topology was always the most common, and that substitutions on discordant trees and discordant branches occurred in only a fraction of the loci underlying the continuous trait.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a description of the simulation conditions.

claim: Substitutions on discordant trees and discordant branches occurred in only a fraction of the loci underlying the continuous trait.
source: We emphasize that the aforementioned effects were observed despite the fact that the concordant topology was always the most common, and that substitutions on discordant trees and discordant branches occurred in only a fraction of the loci underlying the continuous trait.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a description of the simulation conditions.

claim: A positive correlation exists between the estimated σ2 under BM and ILS.
source: Indeed, we observed a positive correlation between the estimated σ2 under BM and ILS (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 6a.

claim: Estimates of Pagel's λ decreased on average with increasing ILS.
source: As expected, estimates of λ decreased on average with increasing ILS (Figure 6b), reflecting the lower phylogenetic signal of traits partly determined by discordant gene trees.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 6b.

claim: Evolutionary rates were much lower when estimated in the presence of λ, but still remain higher in data sets simulated with increasing levels of ILS.
source: Indeed, evolutionary rates were much lower when estimated in the presence of λ (Figure 6c, 'With λ'), but still remain higher in data sets simulated with increasing levels of ILS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 6c.

claim: λ can absorb the effect of hemiplasy by shrinking internal branches, but cannot account for the DC effect resulting from the increased average gene tree heights in higher ILS conditions.
source: This is because while λ can absorb the effect of hemiplasy by shrinking internal branches, it cannot account for the DC effect resulting from the increased average gene tree heights in higher ILS conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation in the results section.

claim: Both the DC effect and hemiplasy contribute to the increase in estimates of σ2.
source: These results suggest that both the DC effect and hemiplasy contribute to the increase in estimates of σ2.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The effect of hemiplasy is comparable to the DC effect, and possibly of even greater magnitude in the presence of more ILS.
source: But our results also suggest that the effect of hemiplasy is comparable to the DC effect, and possibly of even greater magnitude in the presence of more ILS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Larger ancestral population sizes and genealogical discordance can lead to an overestimation of σ2 and to lower values of λ.
source: Assuming that quantitative traits evolve according to the coalescent model, larger ancestral population sizes and genealogical discordance can thus lead to an overestimation of σ2 and to lower values of λ, and will likely affect all comparative methods that can make use of such parameters, not just the BM model.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: A positive correlation exists between ILS levels and the mean number of times the null hypothesis was rejected in the phylogenetic ANOVA.
source: As predicted, we observed a positive correlation between ILS levels and the mean number of times the null hypothesis was rejected in the phylogenetic ANOVA; this trend was unaffected by the number of loci underlying the trait (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: The trend of increased false positive rate in phylogenetic ANOVA was unaffected by the number of loci underlying the trait.
source: As predicted, we observed a positive correlation between ILS levels and the mean number of times the null hypothesis was rejected in the phylogenetic ANOVA; this trend was unaffected by the number of loci underlying the trait (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: Counts of incongruent informative trait patterns increased with increasing ILS levels.
source: As expected, counts of incongruent informative trait patterns increased with increasing ILS levels (Figure 8); congruent trait patterns likewise decreased.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 8.

claim: Congruent trait patterns decreased with increasing ILS levels.
source: As expected, counts of incongruent informative trait patterns increased with increasing ILS levels (Figure 8); congruent trait patterns likewise decreased.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 8.

claim: The same trend of increasing incongruent patterns was observed from simulations where the liability character was underlain by few or many loci.
source: Furthermore, the same trend was observed from simulations where the liability character was underlain by few or many loci (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated in Figure 8.

claim: Even in the case of threshold traits, larger numbers of loci comprising the genetic architecture will not mitigate the effect of hemiplasy.
source: This suggests that even in the case of threshold traits, larger numbers of loci comprising the genetic architecture will not mitigate the effect of hemiplasy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the threshold trait simulation results.

claim: The more genealogical discordance is present in a data set, the more likely it is that a discrete trait will exhibit an incongruent pattern by chance.
source: Overall, the more genealogical discordance is present in a data set, the more likely it is that a discrete trait will exhibit an incongruent pattern by chance, simply as a result of the stochasticity of the coalescent process.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the threshold trait simulation results.

claim: In the absence of ILS the coalescent and traditional BM model are equivalent with respect to the expected covariances between species trait values.
source: By employing coalescent theory, we demonstrate that in the absence of ILS the coalescent and traditional BM model are equivalent with respect to the expected covariances between species trait values, but differ in terms of the species expected trait variances.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: In the absence of ILS the coalescent and traditional BM model differ in terms of the species expected trait variances.
source: By employing coalescent theory, we demonstrate that in the absence of ILS the coalescent and traditional BM model are equivalent with respect to the expected covariances between species trait values, but differ in terms of the species expected trait variances.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: In the presence of ILS, hemiplasy causes the expected covariance in trait values between pairs of more distantly related species to increase.
source: In the presence of ILS, hemiplasy causes the expected covariance in trait values between pairs of more distantly related species to increase.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: Hemiplasy consistently led to an overestimation of σ2.
source: The increased covariance due to hemiplasy leads to error in estimates of two parameters commonly studied under the BM model, namely, the evolutionary rate, σ2, and Pagel's λ. Hemiplasy consistently led to an overestimation of σ2, and to lower λ estimates.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: Hemiplasy led to lower λ estimates.
source: The increased covariance due to hemiplasy leads to error in estimates of two parameters commonly studied under the BM model, namely, the evolutionary rate, σ2, and Pagel's λ. Hemiplasy consistently led to an overestimation of σ2, and to lower λ estimates.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: Hemiplasy affects the number of times threshold traits appeared incongruent with the species tree.
source: Finally, by treating quantitative traits as a liability character underlying a threshold trait, we found that hemiplasy affects the number of times such traits appeared incongruent with the species tree.
evidence: This is stated as a summary finding in the discussion.

claim: ILS is expected to act when there are short internode distances in a species tree, regardless of how far in the past the rapid succession of speciation events has occurred.
source: ILS is expected to act when there are short internode distances in a species tree, regardless of how far in the past the rapid succession of speciation events has occurred.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a general principle.

claim: The effects of hemiplasy will be greatest for species radiations.
source: This implies that the effects of hemiplasy will be greatest for species radiations, as these are defined as periods of rapid speciation (Schluter et al., 1997; Freckleton and Harvey, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Thinning species from analyses in order to minimize or remove discordance can improve the accuracy of inferences about molecular changes.
source: This latter approach — thinning species from analyses in order to minimize or remove discordance — can improve the accuracy of inferences about molecular changes (Mendes and Hahn, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Using Pagel's λ in analyses aimed at estimating evolutionary rates under the BM model will 'buffer' the effect of hemiplasy, minimizing the overall impact of genealogical discordance over the estimates.
source: Another recommendation for avoiding the problems associated with discordance would be to use Pagel's λ in analyses aimed at estimating evolutionary rates under the BM model. We have shown here that Pagel's λ will 'buffer' the effect of hemiplasy, minimizing the overall impact of genealogical discordance over the estimates.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation in the discussion based on the simulation results.

claim: Simulations were conducted with the coalescent simulator ms.
source: Simulations were conducted with the coalescent simulator ms (Hudson, 2002) along species trees ((A:1,B:1):4,C:5) and ((((A:1,B:1):4,C:5):4,D:9):4,E:13).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Parameter estimation was carried out using the 'fitContinuous' function of R's geiger package.
source: We estimated the evolutionary rate, σ2, and λ parameters with the 'fitContinuous' function of R's geiger package (Harmon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a supporting citation.

claim: Phylogenetic ANOVA was conducted using the geiger package.
source: Again, phylogenetic ANOVA was carried out with the geiger package.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
